The core keeps a little leftover magnetism. Spinning makes a weak current, which goes through the field coils and makes the field stronger, which makes more current... it builds itself up in seconds (the 'dynamo-electric principle').

Permanent magnets of the 1860s were weak, so magneto machines could only turn part of the engine's power into electricity. Electromagnet fields made big generators possible — Wheatstone and Varley found the same idea in the same months. Energy is still conserved: double the electricity needs double the steam.
message.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_d: Installed the self-excited dynamo: output x2
This generator already has a self-excited dynamo
This generator already has an electromagnet field built in
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.no: Steam spins a fan really fast. This is how most power plants still work.

Parsons 1884. Coal + water -> 500 kW. One coal lasts 18 s (9 MJ = 30% of the coal's heat; the steam engine gets 5%). Water: a bucket in the top slot (1 bucket = 2 coal), or a water source block beside it feeds it forever. Enough to run the Acheson furnace (500 kW) by itself.

No piston going back and forth, just a wheel of blades turning in one direction — so it can spin fast (Parsons' first: 18,000 rpm) and be built huge. Power plants sit by rivers and the sea because they need lots of cooling water.

Real plants are multi-stage (steam expands through many rows of blades) and use a condenser to turn the steam back into water under vacuum, which raises efficiency. Coal plants reach about 33-40% today, combined-cycle gas plants over 60%. Your electricity is still mostly made by spinning turbines.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.pl: Simplified: blades are not machined on a lathe ([8-01] not yet implemented); single stage, no condenser; feedwater from a river is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_acid_batter: The same kind of battery as in a car. It stores electricity as a chemical change.

Planté 1859. Lead plates in sulfuric acid. Holds 1 MJ. Every face both charges and discharges (up to 10 kW each; only 85% of the charge is stored). On a cable network it charges when there is spare power and discharges when machines need more. Keeps its charge when broken. Right-click: charge level. Glows while discharging.

Charging: 2PbSO4 + 2H2O -> Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. Discharging runs it backwards, so the acid gets weaker as the battery empties — mechanics check charge by measuring the acid's density. Planté made the PbO2 plate by charging and discharging bare lead sheets over and over ('forming').

The first rechargeable battery, and still in nearly every car 160+ years later because it can give a huge current to the starter motor and is cheap and recyclable (over 95% of the lead is recycled). Pure lead plates are soft, so grids were hardened with a few % antimony ([1-43]). Overcharging splits water into H2 + O2 — battery rooms need ventilation.
Simplified: no self-discharge, no voltage (12 V etc.); the case is glass (real: glass jars, later hard rubber / plastic).
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.network: Cable network: %s cables, longest path %s (loss %s%%), %s generators, %s machines, %s batteries, %s delivered
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Joins machines into one electric grid. Long cables lose more power.

Real loss is P = I^2 R: doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power and cuts the loss to a quarter. That is why power lines run at hundreds of kV (transformer [4-10]). In this mod the whole network shares one 1 MW limit (like one trunk line) and the loss uses the longest path for every machine - both are simplifications.
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: Copper wound round and round. It heats metal without touching it - the same principle as an induction (IH) cooktop.

High-frequency AC in the coil induces eddy currents (currents swirling inside the metal), and the metal heats itself through its own resistance (P = I²R). The higher the frequency, the more the current crowds to the surface (skin effect: depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ)).

The principle is Faraday's electromagnetic induction (1831). Practical high-frequency induction furnaces came in the 1920s from Edwin Northrup in the USA. Real coils are hollow copper tubes with cooling water flowing inside, because the coil itself heats up from the current.
item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Spins using electricity. There is one in every fan and washing machine.

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (F = BIL, the Lorentz force). A coil is pushed round by it, and the commutator (a switching part) keeps flipping the current direction. It is the same machine as a dynamo, just run the other way.

Faraday first made a wire circle a magnet using current in 1821. At the 1873 Vienna Exhibition, workers connected two Gramme dynamos and one began to spin as a motor, showing that a generator can also be a motor.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note1: A stone that grabs iron. The ancestor of the compass.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note3: Inside magnetite, small magnetic domains (regions whose magnetism points one way) face random directions. The strong field from a lightning current is thought to line them up, turning the whole stone into a magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note4: The Japanese word jishaku comes from the Chinese "loving stone", which pulls iron like a mother hugging her child. In Han-dynasty China a lodestone spoon called sinan pointed south. In 1600 William Gilbert wrote in De Magnete that the Earth itself is a great magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note1: Spin it and electricity appears, like a bicycle light.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note3: A changing magnetic flux through a coil makes a voltage: EMF = −dΦ/dt (Faraday's law). A spinning coil gives alternating voltage, but the commutator swaps the connections every half turn to give direct current, which electrolysis needs.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note4: In 1832, the year after Faraday's discovery, Pixii in Paris built a hand-cranked magnet generator. Gramme's ring dynamo of 1871 finally gave smooth direct current usable in factories.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite is carbon atoms in stacked hexagonal sheets (sp2 bonds). Electrons free to move within the sheets (π electrons) let it conduct, but with far more resistance than metals (around 1000 times), so current heats it by Joule heating, P = I²R.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: A wire's resistance is R = ρL/A (longer means more, thicker means less). Copper's resistivity is about 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, second only to silver. Wire copper is electrolytically refined to 99.99%, because even small impurities raise the resistance a lot.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Flowing water turns the wheel to make electricity.
Hydro power P = ρgQHη (ρ: water density, g: gravity, Q: flow, H: head, η: efficiency). One tonne of water per second falling 10 m gives about 98 kW, with no fuel burned and no CO2.

The world's first hydroelectric plant opened in Appleton, USA, in 1882. In Japan a spinning mill at Sankyozawa, Sendai, started one in 1888, and Kyoto's Keage plant (1891, on the Lake Biwa Canal) powered Japan's first electric tram in 1895.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Burns coal to boil water and makes electricity from the steam.

Heat engines have a ceiling (Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, in kelvin). With steam at about 150 °C (423 K) and a 40 °C (313 K) cold side the limit is about 26%; real engines lose more to leaks and friction. In this game one coal (30 MJ) gives 1.5 MJ of electricity (5%).

Newcomen's engine (1712) was about 1% efficient. In 1769 Watt multiplied that with a separate condenser (cooling the steam in another vessel). The unit of power, the watt, is named after him, and he invented "horsepower" to sell his engines.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.n: A glass bell on an iron plate. Pump the air out with a hand pump next to it.

Holds a pressure (Pa). Starts at 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. A hand pump next to it lowers the pressure each stroke (down to 1 kPa); a Sprengel mercury pump takes it down to 0.05 Pa. Air slowly leaks back in through the greased seal (about 0.1 Pa per minute). You cannot see the pressure - use a mercury gauge.

19th-century labs used a glass bell jar ground flat at the rim and greased onto a flat plate. The outside air pushes the bell down with about 1 kg on every square centimetre, which is what keeps it sealed.
Large or hot chambers later became welded mild steel, and ultra-high vacuum uses stainless steel baked at 150-250 C so gas trapped in the walls comes out first. Here only the glass stage exists.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.p: Omitted: the grease on the ground seal (tallow [2-09]).
message.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber: You can't see air pressure. Hold a mercury vacuum gauge and right-click.
block.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pump: Magdeburg hemispheres: with the air pumped out, 16 horses could not pull them apart.

Otto von Guericke's air pump (c. 1650). Place next to a vacuum chamber and right-click with an empty hand: each stroke removes 20% of the air (chamber : cylinder = 4 : 1). It never gets below about 1 kPa (1/100 atm). Costs a little hunger.

Each stroke follows Boyle's law: the chamber air spreads into the empty cylinder, the valve closes, and that share is pushed outside. The pressure falls like 0.8, 0.64, 0.51... so the first strokes do the most.

The limit comes from dead volume: air left in the gap between the piston and the valve at the end of the stroke expands back in, and the leather packing leaks. Guericke reached roughly a few hundred Pa to 1 kPa. Better vacuum needed Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) and the diffusion pump (1915).
Approximation: the real cylinder was cast brass/bronze ([1-05] not implemented) - steel here. The leather packing uses vanilla leather (rubber [2-29] not implemented).
message.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pu: Place a vacuum chamber next to the pump.
Whoosh... the piston still moves easily (lots of air left)
Whoosh... very heavy - the air outside pushes back on the piston
It won't go lower - this is the hand pump's limit (about 1 kPa)
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum_ga: Air pressure equals the weight of 76 cm of mercury.

A closed-end U-tube of mercury (Torricelli's mercury column, 1643). Right-click a vacuum chamber: the difference in mercury height is the pressure in mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa, 1 atm = 760 mmHg). Below 1 mm it can't be read by eye.
One arm is sealed with nothing above the mercury (the 'Torricellian vacuum'); the other is open to the chamber. The chamber gas pushes its side down by exactly its pressure in mm of mercury.

For lower pressures came the McLeod gauge (1874, compresses a sample of gas with mercury so it can be read), the Pirani gauge (1906, how fast a hot wire cools) and the hot-cathode ionization gauge (1916, built like a vacuum tube).
message.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum: The mercury levels are within 1 mm - too low to read (below %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Everything is inside the glass, but it is still full of air. Seal it on a sealing station.
Glass bulb + tungsten wire filament + iron wire grid + iron plate. With air inside, the hot filament would burn out at once. Put it in a sealing station next to a pumped-down vacuum chamber.
Approximation: grid and plate are iron (nickel [1-37] not implemented). The lead-in wires through the glass (platinum / Dumet wire, glass-metal seal [5-12]) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note1: Add one more electrode to a light bulb and you can control the flow of electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note: Lee de Forest's Audion (1906). The hot tungsten filament boils off electrons; the plate collects them; a small voltage on the grid between them controls a large current - an amplifier. Part of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note3: Fleming's diode (1904) used Edison's discovery that a hot filament gives off current. De Forest added the zig-zag grid. Before transistors, every radio, telephone repeater and early computer amplified with tubes like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note4: De Forest's first Audions were 'soft' - gas left inside made them erratic. Langmuir and Arnold (c. 1913) showed that a hard vacuum (about 10^-4 Pa) makes tubes stable, which needed diffusion pumps and getters (the silver film inside a tube is the getter that ate the last gas).
Pump the air out of the bulb, then melt the glass neck shut.

Place next to a vacuum chamber (it is the exhaust manifold). Tube assembly + chamber at 0.1 Pa or lower + 500 W x 10 s (filament heated to drive out gas) -> triode vacuum tube. A hand pump cannot reach 0.1 Pa - you need a Sprengel mercury pump. Each tube lets some air back into the chamber (5% of the gap to 1 atm) - wait for it to pump down again.

Real tube factories pumped each bulb through a glass tube at its top, heated the parts to drive out gas, then melted that tube shut with a flame. The little glass tip on old tubes and light bulbs is where it was sealed off.

Gas hides in the metal and glass surfaces. While pumping, the filament is run hot and the plate heated (later by induction) so the gas comes out before sealing; finally the getter is flashed to absorb what is left.
Approximation: the sealing-off flame (gas burner) is represented by electric power.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Tungsten only emits electrons (thermionic emission) above about 2000 °C. At that temperature in air it burns at once: 2W + 3O2 → 2WO3 (yellow smoke). Gas molecules would also get in the electrons' way.

De Forest's 1906 triode, the Audion, still held some gas (a "soft" vacuum) and behaved erratically. Around 1913 Langmuir and others pumped tubes to a high vacuum and made them stable. The silver mirror inside later tubes is the getter (barium) that soaks up leftover gas.
block.semiconductor-lab.sprengel_pump.no: A pump that carries air away bit by bit with falling drops of mercury.

Place it next to a vacuum chamber and load 4 mercury: it keeps pumping every second (no power, mercury is not used up). It reaches 0.05 Pa; at 0.1 Pa or below the sealing station can seal vacuum tubes. Roughing to 1 kPa with the hand pump first is a little faster.

Mercury drops falling down a narrow glass tube trap pockets of gas between them and push them down like little pistons. With no moving parts and no dead space it reaches pressures about ten thousand times lower than a hand pump - though the mercury's own vapour (about 0.2 Pa at 20 °C) remains.

Invented by Hermann Sprengel in London in 1865; his first pump emptied a half-litre vessel in about 20 minutes. In 1879 Swan and Edison exhausted their carbon-filament lamps with it, so the filaments glowed for a long time instead of burning out. Crookes ran several in series to study cathode rays in his discharge tubes - a path that led to the discovery of the electron.

block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Put sulfuric acid or salt in the lower-left slot. (1) Water + sulfuric acid (not used up): 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, 572 kJ = 115 s at 5 kW. (2) Water + 2 salt [6-05]: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH, about 640 kJ = 128 s. The + electrode gives oxygen from water, chlorine from brine.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: H2, made by splitting water. One bag ≈ 1 mol (≈24 L at 25 °C, 1 atm). 19th-century labs carried gases in rubberised-cloth bags. Store large amounts in a Gas Holder [6-02]. Later used as a protective furnace atmosphere and for ammonia (Haber–Bosch).
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note: O2, from the + electrode of the electrolyzer, half the volume of the hydrogen. One bag ≈ 1 mol. Keep it in a different holder from hydrogen: mixed, they make an explosive oxyhydrogen mixture. Later used for oxidising silicon (SiO2 film).
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: The lightest gas. A balloon filled with it floats up into the sky.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note1: The gas that makes things burn. About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note1: In the age of gas lamps, gas tanks were sealed with water so the gas could not leak out.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note: A low-pressure tank: a bottomless iron bell over a tank of water (19th-century gasworks). Gas lifts the bell, and the bell's weight pushes the gas out. Holds one gas at a time (set by the first gas in, cleared when empty). Automatically takes the same gas from an adjacent electrolyzer. Capacity 1000 mol ≈ 24.5 m³ (25 °C, 1 atm). Mixing hydrogen and oxygen gives oxyhydrogen (2H2+O2→2H2O): bang.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note3: London's Gas Light and Coke Company (founded 1812) stored coal gas in water-sealed gasholders and piped it to street lamps. The huge cylindrical iron frames still stand at places like King's Cross, reused as a park and as flats.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note4: Gas pressure = bell weight ÷ bell area (a few kPa, a few % above atmospheric), so no compressor is needed, but the volume stays large. Squeezing gas small enough to carry is the job of the compressor and cylinder [6-03]. Hydrogen molecules are tiny and slowly escape through gaps in metal and dissolve a little in the seal water (ignored in game).
item.semiconductor-lab.empty_gas_cylinde: A thick steel bottle that can hold gas squeezed to 150 times air pressure.

A seamless steel cylinder (about 10 L). Put it in a compressor next to a gas holder: it is filled with 50 mol of that gas at about 150 atm. Low-pressure bags (about 1 mol) are still handy for small amounts.

Gas cylinders became practical in the 1880s: Brin's Oxygen Company in London (1886) sold compressed oxygen in metal cylinders, and the Mannesmann brothers' seamless steel tubes (late 1880s) made strong cylinders without a welded seam.
50 mol at 25 C and 150 atm takes V = nRT/P = 50 x 0.0821 x 298 / 150, about 8 L (ideal gas). Real cylinders are tested with water at 5/3 of the filling pressure and re-tested every few years.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_cylinder: In Japan, hydrogen cylinders are painted red so nobody mixes them up.
50 mol of H2 compressed to about 150 atm in a steel cylinder (about 1.2 m3 of gas at normal pressure). Flammable: 4-75% in air can explode.
Japan's High Pressure Gas Safety Act fixes cylinder colours: oxygen black, hydrogen red, carbon dioxide green, chlorine yellow, ammonia white, acetylene brown, others grey.

Hydrogen atoms are so small that they creep into steel and make it brittle (hydrogen embrittlement). Hydrogen cylinders use tougher, lower-strength steel, and modern 700-bar fuel-cell car tanks use carbon fibre with a plastic liner. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_cylinder.n: In Japan, oxygen cylinders are painted black.
50 mol of O2 compressed to about 150 atm. Pure oxygen makes things burn violently: never put oil or grease on the valve.
The first big use of bottled oxygen was the limelight of theatres (an oxy-hydrogen flame heating lime) and then welding and cutting with the oxy-acetylene torch (1903). Hospitals followed.

At high pressure, oil and grease can ignite by themselves in oxygen (adiabatic compression heats the gas when a valve is opened quickly). Oxygen valves are cleaned to remove oil and opened slowly. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note1: High-pressure cylinders were made in the 1880s, and people could carry gas around.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note: An electric piston compressor. Place it next to a gas holder with at least 50 mol: empty cylinder + 50 mol + 5 kW x 124 s -> filled cylinder of that gas. The energy (620 kJ) is the work to squeeze 50 mol from 1 to 150 atm at constant temperature, nRT ln(150).
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note3: Squeezing gas heats it, so real compressors work in stages (for example 1 -> 6 -> 30 -> 150 atm) with water coolers between them. A bicycle pump gets warm for the same reason.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note4: Isothermal work W = nRT ln(P2/P1) = 50 x 8.314 x 298 x ln150, about 621 kJ. Squeezing to 150 atm in one adiabatic stroke (no cooling) would need more work (about 1 MJ) and heat the gas to nearly 1000 C, which is why multi-stage cooling matters.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note1: Salt that turned into stone. It used to be a sea.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note2: Halite, NaCl 95-99%. Found in evaporite beds under deserts and badlands. Crush it in the crafting grid to get salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note3: When an ancient sea was cut off and dried up, its salts settled in layers. Salt beds can be hundreds of metres thick. Poland's Wieliczka mine has been worked since the 13th century and even has a chapel carved out of salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note4: Seawater precipitates salts in order as it evaporates: calcite -> gypsum -> halite -> potassium/magnesium salts. That is why rock salt beds often sit on top of gypsum. Salt is soft and flows slowly under pressure, forming salt domes that trap oil.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.placeho: Approximation: crushing gives salt 1:1. Removing impurities (gypsum, clay) by dissolving and recrystallising is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note1: The same salt you eat. Rock salt and sea salt are both NaCl.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note2: Sodium chloride NaCl. Raw material for chlor-alkali electrolysis [6-05] (brine -> chlorine + hydrogen + caustic soda).
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note3: Salt was so valuable that Roman soldiers were said to receive a salt allowance - the word 'salary' is often linked to it. In Japan, salt was made from seawater because there is no rock salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note4: Today about 40% of the salt mined worldwide goes to the chemical industry, mostly to chlor-alkali plants. Japan has no rock salt, so it imports solar salt from Mexico and Australia for that.
block.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt_ore.no: A layer of salt deep under the desert. Long ago this was a sea.
Evaporite bed. Generates only under deserts and badlands (y0-48), replacing stone in large lenses. Soft (Mohs 2.5): any pickaxe drops rock salt; silk touch keeps the block.
Rock salt is 'a sea turned into stone'. The Zechstein sea dried up about 255 million years ago and left salt under much of northern Europe.
Salt mines are dry and stable, so some old ones store nuclear waste or archives. Salt also conducts heat well and seals cracks by slowly flowing.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.pla: Simplified (brine mode): the diaphragm / mercury cell / ion-exchange membrane that keeps chlorine away from the caustic soda is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_gas.note: A yellow-green, poisonous gas. Salt and electricity make it.

Cl2, from the + electrode when brine is electrolysed [6-05]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Store it in a gas holder (mixing with hydrogen explodes: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl). Burn it with hydrogen to make hydrochloric acid [6-06].

Scheele made chlorine in 1774 from hydrochloric acid and manganese dioxide but thought it contained oxygen. In 1810 Davy showed it was an element and named it after the Greek 'chloros' (yellow-green).

Chlorine is heavier than air (2.5x), so it sinks into hollows. It became the first large-scale chemical weapon at Ypres in 1915 - and also the chlorination of drinking water (from 1908) that saved far more lives.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_cylinder: In Japan, chlorine cylinders are painted yellow.
50 mol of Cl2 filled by the compressor [6-03] from a gas holder.
Chlorine turns into a liquid at only about 7 atm at room temperature, so real chlorine cylinders contain liquid chlorine with gas on top - much more fits than in a hydrogen cylinder.

Cylinder colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard: hydrogen red, oxygen black, chlorine yellow. Dry chlorine does not attack steel, but wet chlorine does (it forms HCl), so cylinders must be kept dry.
Caustic soda. Strong enough to dissolve skin - handle with care.
NaOH, collects at the - electrode in brine electrolysis [6-05] (2 per run). Strong base: later used in the Bayer process for alumina [1-14] and for soap.
Chlorine and caustic soda always come out together in a fixed ratio (1 t Cl2 : 1.1 t NaOH). Plants must find buyers for both - this is called the 'chlor-alkali balance'.
Before electrolysis (1890s), caustic soda was made by boiling soda ash with slaked lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3. Castner and Kellner's mercury cell (1892) made electrolysis practical.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note1: Burns hydrogen in chlorine and dissolves the smoke in water to make hydrochloric acid.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note2: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl (burns at about 2000 C), then HCl gas is absorbed in water. 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 + 1/4 bucket of water (5 s) -> 1 hydrochloric acid. Gas from bags (1 mol), cylinders (50 mol) or an adjacent gas holder. No electricity needed. With no water (water slot empty), the HCl stays as dry gas: 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 -> 2 bags of hydrogen chloride gas, for trichlorosilane [1-16].
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note3: Burning hydrogen in chlorine gives a pale flame and white fumes of HCl. This 'synthetic hydrochloric acid' became the main use for the chlorine and hydrogen that chlor-alkali plants produced from the 1890s on.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note4: The burner nozzle is made of quartz (later graphite) because hot HCl eats metals. The mixture is only safe because the gases meet at the nozzle: premixed H2 + Cl2 explodes in sunlight. Earlier, HCl came from the Leblanc process (salt + sulfuric acid) and was simply vented as a pollutant until the 1863 Alkali Act.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.place: Approximation: one-block burner with a built-in absorber. Gas amounts are stoichiometric; cooling water is not needed.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrochloric_acid: A strong acid that dissolves metals. Your stomach makes a weak version of it.
HCl dissolved in water (about 25%, 2 mol HCl per bottle). Made in the HCl synthesis burner [6-06]. Used for tungstic acid [1-28] and germanium tetrachloride [1-34].
Alchemists called it 'spirit of salt' (made by heating salt with sulfuric acid). Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off HCl gas that fumes in moist air. Gastric juice is about 0.1 mol/L HCl.

HCl gas dissolves enormously in water: about 450 L of gas per litre at 20 C, so you cannot make it more than about 38%. In semiconductor fabs, dilute HCl with hydrogen peroxide (RCA clean SC-2, 1965) removes metal contamination from wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: Burning makes only water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, releasing about 286 kJ per bag (1 mol), exactly the electricity the electrolyzer spent splitting it. Mixed with air at 4-75% it explodes when lit.

Cavendish discovered it in 1766 as the "inflammable air" given off when acid meets metal. In 1783 Lavoisier named it hydrogène, "water-maker"; the Japanese name suiso (water element) translates that. The same year Charles flew in a hydrogen balloon.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note3: In sulfuric-acid electrolysis, + electrode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; − electrode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H2. Four electrons give one O2 and two H2, so the oxygen is half the hydrogen's volume.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note4: Scheele and Priestley each discovered it in the 1770s. Lavoisier thought every acid contained it and named it oxygène, "acid-maker". That was wrong (hydrochloric acid, HCl, has no oxygen), but the Japanese name sanso (acid element) keeps the mistake alive.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Pure water barely conducts, so sulfuric acid is added to supply ions (charged particles that carry current); the acid itself is not used up. Splitting water needs 1.23 V in theory, but about 2 V in practice because of losses at the electrodes.

In 1800, just after news of Volta's pile arrived, Nicholson and Carlisle electrolyzed water. In 1834 Faraday found the laws of electrolysis and coined (with Whewell's help) the words electrode, anode, cathode, ion and electrolyte.
block.semiconductor-lab.air_separation_u: Freezes air into a liquid and splits it into nitrogen, oxygen and argon.

Runs on electricity alone (the raw material is the air around it). 5 kW x 16 s separates 10 mol of air: about 8 bags of nitrogen, 2 of oxygen, and one bag of argon every ~11 runs. A gas holder next to it pulls from the outputs automatically.

Air is compressed to about 200 atm, cooled in a heat exchanger and then expanded through a small valve, which cools it (the Joule-Thomson effect). Repeating this liquefies it at about -194 °C. Distilling the liquid air stage by stage in a rectifying column sends low-boiling nitrogen (-196 °C) up and oxygen (-183 °C) down, while argon (-186 °C) collects in the middle.

Carl von Linde liquefied air in 1895 and separated oxygen with a rectifying column in 1902. Argon had been found in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, because nitrogen from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made chemically. Its name is Greek for 'lazy' (it reacts with nothing). It later filled light bulbs and the furnaces that pull silicon crystals. Early plants used far more electricity than today's.
Omitted: the insulated cold box (real ones were wooden boxes packed with wool etc.), hours of cool-down at start-up, a separate argon column. Power uses the modern value (1900s plants used more).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_gas.note: Four fifths of the air is this gas. Breathing it in does nothing to your body.

N2. Comes from the air separation unit [6-07]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Works with gas holders and the compressor (nitrogen cylinder). It reacts with almost nothing, so it is used to blanket things you do not want oxidized.

The two atoms of N2 are held by a triple bond (N≡N, about 945 kJ/mol), so it hardly reacts at ordinary temperatures. Above about 1200 °C, though, it reacts with silicon to form silicon nitride (Si3N4) - so molten silicon is blanketed with argon instead.

Discovered in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford as air in which neither a candle nor a mouse could live. Lavoisier called it azote, 'lifeless' (still its French name). Plants cannot use nitrogen from the air directly; until the Haber-Bosch process [6-09] turned it into fertilizer, it set the limit on food.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note1: A gas that reacts with nothing, about 1% of the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note2: Ar. The air separation unit gives one bag per about 108 mol of air. Works with gas holders and the compressor (argon cylinder). Planned use: filling the furnace that pulls silicon crystals (CZ).
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note3: Argon is a noble gas (group 18): its outer electron shell is exactly full, so it bonds with almost nothing. Molten silicon (1414 °C) reacts with nitrogen and oxygen, but not with argon. It is about 1.4 times denser than air and lingers even in an open container.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note4: Discovered in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, who noticed that 'nitrogen' left after removing oxygen etc. from air was about 0.5% heavier than nitrogen made by chemical reactions. It is 0.93% of the air, yet nobody had noticed. Almost all argon on Earth comes from the decay of potassium-40 in rocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_cylinder: In Japan, nitrogen cylinders are painted grey.
50 mol of N2 from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Nitrogen cannot be liquefied at room temperature however hard you squeeze it (it stays gas above its critical temperature, -147 °C). So the cylinder holds high-pressure gas; liquid nitrogen travels in insulated vacuum flasks.

The Japanese rules fix the colours for oxygen (black), hydrogen (red), liquefied CO2 (green), liquefied ammonia (white), liquefied chlorine (yellow) and acetylene (brown). Every other gas, nitrogen and argon included, is grey with the contents written on it.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_cylinder.no: Argon cylinders are grey too - read the lettering to tell them apart.
50 mol of Ar from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Argon's critical temperature is -122 °C, so like nitrogen it is high-pressure gas, not liquid, in a room-temperature cylinder. It is the most common shielding gas that protects metal from air during welding.

Argon comes out of air separation alongside oxygen and nitrogen, so it is by far the cheapest noble gas. It is inside light bulbs too: it slows the evaporation of the tungsten filament (Langmuir filled bulbs with nitrogen in 1913, later argon).
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note: Fused silica (pure SiO2) survives high heat and adds no impurities. Ordinary glass would melt and leak sodium.
block.semiconductor-lab.oxyhydrogen_burn: Burn hydrogen and oxygen together and the flame gets hot enough to melt quartz.

Connect a hydrogen cylinder and an oxygen cylinder ([6-03] compressor). Vein quartz x1 + H2 4 mol + O2 2 mol (10 s) -> fused quartz. 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, flame about 2800 C; quartz (SiO2) melts at about 1713 C. One H2 cylinder = 12.5 quartz, one O2 cylinder = 25 (2:1 ratio). No electricity needed. Empty cylinders come out bottom right.

1801: Robert Hare (USA) built the oxyhydrogen blowpipe and melted platinum for the first time. 1839: Marc Antoine Gaudin (France) melted rock crystal in the flame and drew threads of fused quartz. From 1899 Heraeus (Germany) made fused quartz industrially. The same flame lit theatres as 'limelight' (a block of quicklime glowing in it).

Hare kept the two gases in separate reservoirs and mixed them only at the nozzle tip: premixed H2 + O2 is knallgas and detonates. The flame is almost invisible (pale blue) and gives off only water vapour, so it does not contaminate quartz with carbon or sulfur. Heraeus later moved to electric melting; today synthetic fused silica is made by burning SiCl4 in an H2/O2 flame.
Approx: a 1-block bench burner. Gas per quartz is a game value (assumes ~10% of the flame's heat reaches the quartz). Gas left in the burner is lost if you break it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fused_quartz.note: Quartz melted into clear glass. Heat it red hot, drop it in water, and it still will not crack.
Pure SiO2 glass. Melt vein quartz in the oxyhydrogen burner (~2000 C). A furnace (~1000 C) is far too cold: quartz melts at about 1713 C. Made into quartz tubes for the zone refiner.
Gaudin melted quartz in an oxyhydrogen flame in 1839; Heraeus started industrial production in 1899. Ordinary glass is mostly SiO2 too, but soda and lime are added so it melts at about 1000 C.

Thermal expansion is only about 0.5 x 10^-6 per K (soda-lime glass ~9 x 10^-6), so it survives thermal shock. It transmits UV down to about 160-200 nm, which is why lithography lenses and photomask blanks are fused silica. With no sodium, it does not poison semiconductors.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note1: A glass tube made of the same stuff as rock crystal. It barely minds heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note3: Fused quartz is an almost pure SiO2 network that expands with heat only about 1/20 as much as ordinary glass (about 0.5×10⁻⁶ per K), so a red-hot tube can be dunked in water without cracking. It does not conduct electricity, so the induction coil's field passes straight through and only the germanium inside heats up.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note4: It began in 1839 when Gaudin melted tiny beads of quartz with an oxyhydrogen flame. Clear quartz tubing was first made industrially around 1900 in Germany (Heraeus), again with oxyhydrogen flames. In Pfann's zone refining the graphite boat sat inside a quartz tube filled with protective gas.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass_batch: Sand mixed with lead powder (litharge) and potash. Melted, it becomes a sparkling glass.
5 sand + 1 litharge + 1 potassium carbonate -> 5. By weight roughly SiO2 49%, PbO 36%, K2O 15% (close to real flint glass). Melt in a blast furnace for 20 s to get flint glass.
"Flint" comes from English glassmakers who used burnt, crushed flint pebbles instead of sand. Lead also lowers the melting temperature, making the glass easier to work.

PbO enters the glass network as a modifier. Heavy lead ions have easily distorted electron clouds (high polarizability), so light slows down more and the refractive index rises. Violet light is slowed even more than red, so dispersion grows too.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note1: Heavy, sparkling glass with lead in it. It bends light strongly and splits it into rainbow colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note2: Optical flint (lead glass, about 40% PbO). Refractive index about 1.6, high dispersion (Abbe number about 36-41). Combined with crown glass it makes an achromatic lens [7-04]. Lead is toxic - don't lick it.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note3: In 1674 the Englishman George Ravenscroft patented a clear glass that did not cloud, usually counted as the start of lead crystal (⚠️ historians debate whether his early glass really contained lead). In the 18th century lead glass was used for lenses as flint glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note4: A single lens focuses each color at a different point (chromatic aberration). Cementing a low-dispersion crown convex lens to a high-dispersion flint concave lens keeps the bending power but cancels the color error (Hall c. 1733, Dollond 1758). Lithography projection lenses also combine many glass types to cancel color and shape errors.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.place: Omitted: removing bubbles and striae. Represented by the long melt time in the blast furnace (20 s).
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note1: Glass remade evenly for lenses. It hardly splits light into colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note2: Soda-lime glass remelted in a blast furnace and stirred to remove striae: optical glass. Refractive index about 1.52, low dispersion (Abbe number about 59). Combined with flint glass it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note3: The name comes from old window-glass making: a blown glass bubble was spun out into a flat disc (a 'crown'). Around 1805 the Swiss Guinand stirred molten glass with a fireclay rod to make optical glass free of bubbles and striae, and worked with Fraunhofer in Germany.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note4: The Abbe number measures how little a glass spreads colors: the larger, the less color fringing. In 1884 Abbe, Schott and Zeiss set up a works in Jena and created new optical glasses with boron and barium. Today's standard lens glass BK7 is also a borosilicate crown.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.place: Approximation: real optical crown is potash-lime or borosilicate glass (BK7). Here it is made from soda-lime glass (soda crown). Stirring is represented by the blast-furnace time (20 s).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note1: A red powder made by roasting iron. It is so fine that it can polish glass to a shine.
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note2: Iron nugget -> furnace (roasted in air) -> iron(III) oxide Fe2O3. Used with the pitch lap to polish a ground lens clear.
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note3: Red iron oxide has been a pigment since ancient times and was jeweller's rouge for polishing gems and metals. Newton polished his mirror with putty (tin oxide), but in the 19th century Lord Rosse used red iron oxide (⚠️ when it was first used for lenses is unconfirmed).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note4: From the 1940s cerium oxide CeO2 took over (⚠️). CeO2 does not just scrape: it bonds chemically with the SiO2 of the glass and pulls the surface away, so it polishes fast and flat (the idea behind chemical mechanical polishing, CMP, used to flatten chips today).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.placeholder: Approximation: real jeweller's rouge was often made by roasting green vitriol (iron sulfate). Here iron is roasted in air (the old crocus martis method).
item.semiconductor-lab.grinding_tool.not: An iron dish for grinding glass with sand into a lens shape. It can be used again and again.
3 iron ingots. Put it in the crafting grid with optical glass and sand to get a frosted lens blank (the tool comes back).
17th-century lens makers rubbed glass on a hollow iron or brass dish with wet sand or emery (corundum powder), changing from coarse to fine powder in many steps.

Rubbing two surfaces together in all directions wears down the high spots until they become spherical (the sphere is the only shape that fits itself however it slides). That is why old lenses were almost all spherical.
item.semiconductor-lab.grinding_tool.pla: Omitted: the many grinding steps from coarse sand to fine emery and the gauges that set the radius. The tool does not wear.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note1: An iron dish covered with soft pitch, for polishing lenses. It can be used again and again.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note2: 3 pitch + iron ingot. Put it in the crafting grid with a ground lens blank and rouge to get a clear lens (the lap comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note3: A hard tool scratches. Pitch slowly flows to match the lens exactly and presses the polishing grains gently. Newton also wrote about polishing his mirror on pitch.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note4: The shape of a polished surface is checked with Newton's rings, the interference fringes seen when a reference surface is laid on it. One fringe means a difference of half a wavelength (about 0.3 um). Projection lens [7-19] surfaces are now matched to a few nanometres.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.placeho: Omitted: the lap does not wear. Adjusting the pitch hardness with temperature is also omitted.
Crown glass ground with sand into a convex lens shape. Still frosted and cloudy.
Crown glass + sand + grinding tool (comes back). The surface is full of tiny scratches that scatter light. Polish it with the pitch lap and rouge for a clear lens.
Ground glass looks cloudy because the bumpy surface scatters light in all directions. Wet it and the bumps fill in, so you can see through it a little.
The depth of the scratches left by grinding depends on the grain size. Polishing must remove more than that depth (a few um), which is why the powder is changed to finer and finer grades.
Flint glass ground with sand into a concave lens shape. Still frosted.
Flint glass + sand + grinding tool (comes back). Polish it with the pitch lap and rouge for a clear lens.
Lead glass is softer than ordinary glass and scratches easily, so it must be polished with special care.
A concave lens is ground on a convex tool. Convex and concave tools are rubbed against each other to make a matched pair of the same radius.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note1: A polished, clear convex lens. It brings light to a point, like a magnifying glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note2: Ground crown lens blank + rouge + pitch lap (comes back). Refractive index about 1.52. Combined with a flint concave lens it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note3: Spectacles were invented in Italy in the late 13th century (convex lenses for reading). Lens is Latin for lentil, from the shape.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note4: The focal length f of a convex lens depends on the surface radii and the refractive index (1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)). But n changes with color, so blue focuses nearer and red farther (chromatic aberration).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note1: A polished, clear concave lens. It spreads light out.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note2: Ground flint lens blank + rouge + pitch lap (comes back). Refractive index about 1.6, strong color spreading. Cemented to a crown convex lens it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note3: In 1758 Dollond patented an achromatic lens combining a crown convex lens and a flint concave lens (Hall had made one around 1733).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note4: A concave lens alone forms no image, but its color error is opposite to that of a convex lens. Flint spreads colors strongly, so a weak concave flint lens can cancel the crown's color error. The pair stays a convex lens overall, but the color fringes vanish.
item.semiconductor-lab.achromatic_lens.n: Two lenses of different glass put together. The rainbow fringes disappear and the image is sharp.

Crown lens (convex) + flint lens (concave) + copper ingot (lens cell). Low-dispersion crown and high-dispersion flint cancel the color-by-color focus error (chromatic aberration). It becomes the objective of a refracting telescope.
Newton thought color fringes could not be removed with lenses and built a mirror telescope instead. Around 1733 Hall made an achromatic lens, and in 1758 Dollond patented it and made it widespread.

Achromatic means bringing two colors (usually red and blue) to one focus. The small leftover error (secondary spectrum) is reduced further with special materials such as fluorite (apochromats). Lithography projection lenses [7-19] combine many more glasses and use light of a single wavelength to avoid color problems.
item.semiconductor-lab.achromatic_lens.p: Omitted: the cement between the two lenses (Canada balsam from the 19th century). The real cell is brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.refracting_telesc: A tube for seeing far things large. Hold right-click to look through it (like the vanilla spyglass).

Achromatic lens (top, objective) + copper ingot (tube) + crown lens (bottom, eyepiece). Both are convex (Keplerian), so the image is upside down (fine for stars). Magnification = objective focal length / eyepiece focal length.

In 1608 Lippershey in the Netherlands applied for a telescope patent. In 1609 Galileo found mountains on the Moon and four moons of Jupiter with telescopes he made himself. The two-convex-lens design was proposed by Kepler in 1611.

Before achromatic lenses, telescopes were made extremely long so the color fringes were less noticeable. Hevelius's 17th-century telescope was about 45 m long and hung from a mast with ropes. Achromatic lenses made telescopes short and bright.
Approximation: the view (zoom and field) is the same as the vanilla spyglass, and the image is not flipped. The real tube is brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note1: A triangular glass that splits light into rainbow colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note2: Flint glass + sand + grinding tool + rouge + pitch lap (tools come back). Three flat faces are ground and polished. High-dispersion flint spreads the colors widely. The heart of the spectroscope.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note3: In 1666 Newton passed sunlight from a hole in a window shutter through a prism and showed that white light is a mixture of rainbow colors. A second prism passing a single color did not split it further.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note4: Light splits because the refractive index differs by color (dispersion); violet bends most. Ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet (shorter than about 350 nm), so UV spectroscopy uses quartz or fluorite prisms [7-15].
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.note: A tool that splits light into a rainbow to see which colored lines it has. Put something in a flame and look, and you can tell which elements it contains.

Use: hold a sample (salt, potash, slaked lime, boric acid...) in the other hand and right-click a lit campfire or fire -> element lines (flame test). Right-click the air under the open sky by day -> the Sun's dark lines. Recipe: prism + 2 crown lenses + 3 copper ingots.

In 1859 Kirchhoff and Bunsen found that each element gives lines of its own colors (spectral analysis). With it they discovered caesium the next year and rubidium the year after. In 1868 a line from an element unknown on Earth was seen in the Sun during an eclipse: helium.

Electrons in an atom can only sit on fixed energy steps, and stepping down they give off light with exactly the energy difference (a fixed wavelength). So the line positions are fingerprints of elements. The same element also absorbs those wavelengths (the Sun's dark lines). Spectroscopy is still used to find tiny impurities in semiconductor materials.
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.plac: Approximation: the real thing uses the soot-free flame of a Bunsen burner; here a campfire. Only strong visible lines are shown as text.
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.flam: An unbroken rainbow from red to violet (continuous spectrum): hot soot particles glowing
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.hold: -> Hold a sample in your other hand and look at the flame again
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.none: No clear lines (it does not glow at flame temperature, or does not evaporate)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.line: Sodium Na: two bright yellow lines 589.0 nm, 589.6 nm (D lines)
Potassium K: deep red 766.5 nm, 769.9 nm and violet 404.4 nm (lilac flame)
Calcium Ca: orange-red band (~620 nm, CaOH), green band (~554 nm) and violet 422.7 nm
Boron B: green bands ~518 nm, 548 nm (BO2; the flame turns green)
Lead Pb: a weak violet line 405.8 nm (pale bluish flame)
Germanium Ge: its strong line is ultraviolet, 265.1 nm, invisible (glass prisms also block UV)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.sun: ☀ Spectrum of sunlight: many thin dark lines across the rainbow (Fraunhofer lines)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.sun_: C 656.3 nm (hydrogen), D 589 nm (sodium), b 517 nm (magnesium), F 486.1 nm (hydrogen), H/K 396.8/393.4 nm (calcium). Gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those colors
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.no_s: Point it at the air under open sky by day to see sunlight's spectrum (or at a lit campfire)
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note: Moves the coil slowly along the bar. Too fast and impurities cannot keep up.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note1: A long threaded rod: turn it and things move in a straight line.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note3: The distance moved per turn is the lead (pitch). Speed = lead × revolutions. A 1 mm lead screw turned once a minute moves 6 cm an hour, turning a motor's spin into a slow, precise straight-line motion.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note4: Around 1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was driven by a lead screw, so accurate screws could be made identical again and again. The stages of today's chip lithography machines (ball screws) are its descendants.
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.hint: Left: Ge (max 8)  Mid: boat  Right: dopant
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max: Now: %s (limit of zone refining). Add a dopant to make n/p-type
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.ready: Now: %s - transistor grade. Add a dopant, or refine to 10N
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.doping: Zone leveling: spreading dopant evenly through %s germanium
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.no_boat: Put a graphite boat in the middle
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.need_power: No power: the HF oscillator is off
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.clay_cap: Clay boat stops at 9N. 10N: synthetic boat
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.route_cap: Sulfate-route Ge stops at 9N. 10N needs GeCl4
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: Molten germanium does not react with graphite. Silicon does (forms SiC) - which is why Chapter 2 needs a different method.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.not_ge: Only germanium can be zone-refined here. Put in reduced or refined germanium.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max_pu: Already 11N - zone refining cannot go further.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.empty: The furnace is empty. Right-click with germanium to start.
item.semiconductor-lab.refined_germanium: Purity is about the inside of the crystal. The surface gets dirty from your hands and air at once - real labs etch it off with acid (CP-4) right before use. Not yet in the game.
Made by zone leveling: dopant is added to the molten zone so it spreads evenly. Mixing solids would not work.
Made by zone leveling: dopant is added to the molten zone so it spreads evenly. Mixing solids would not work.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: The old 19th-century kind: cheap, but clay impurities seep into the germanium, so it only gets you to 9N.

Clay-graphite crucibles (natural graphite bonded with clay) were the standard for melting metals in the 19th century. For semiconductors the clay (aluminium, iron, alkali metals) is the problem - Bell Labs used high-purity synthetic graphite.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: A boat carved from very clean man-made graphite. Germanium gets all the way to 10N.
Goes in the middle slot of the zone refining furnace and is not used up. With this boat germanium refines to 10N (the clay-graphite boat stops at 9N).
Molten germanium does not wet or react with graphite, so a clean graphite boat adds almost nothing to the bar. Pfann's zone refiners used high-purity graphite boats inside a quartz tube.

Omitted: real boats are machined on a lathe/mill from a graphite block, then purified further by baking in chlorine or freon gas at about 2500 C (metal impurities leave as volatile chlorides). Here 3 synthetic graphite are shaped at the crafting table.
block.semiconductor-lab.zone_refining_fu: Melt only a thin slice of the bar and slide it along: the dirt follows the melt to the end.

Left: germanium (max 8). Middle: graphite boat (not used up; clay-graphite = up to 9N, synthetic = up to 10N). Right: dopant. Runs on electricity: the built-in HF oscillator draws 3 kW (stops without power). 30 s per pass.

The HF oscillator drives the copper coil; the alternating magnetic field induces currents in the germanium itself, so only the part inside the coil melts. The boat and the quartz tube stay cool enough not to contaminate it. (The same principle as an induction cooktop. This furnace is the [3-14] induction furnace of the tech tree.)
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: In Pfann's zone refining (Bell Labs, 1952) the germanium bar rode in a graphite boat through a quartz tube. Molten germanium barely wets graphite, so the bar comes out cleanly after it freezes.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat_bla: A graphite boat before firing. Still soft.
Made from 3 graphite and clay. Fire it in a furnace (or the electric furnace) to get a clay-graphite boat.
Clay (kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4) loses its bound water at around 500 °C and hardens. The clay acts as the glue that holds the graphite grains together.

Clay-graphite crucibles were mass-produced in the 19th century for melting steel and brass; the Morgan company, founded in London in 1856, started out making them. Graphite conducts heat well and is hard for molten metal to wet.
item.semiconductor-lab.junction_transist: A 1950s transistor, much sturdier than the point-contact kind.
Fire the unfired part in a furnace. Three of them make a transistor radio.
A p-n-p structure: a thin n-type Ge base between two indium-soaked p-type layers (emitter and collector). A small base current controls a large emitter-to-collector current - amplification.
Developed around 1951 at GE and RCA. Easy to make, it was widely used in 1950s hearing aids and radios, but the base was hard to make thin, so it was poor at high frequencies.
Germanium sandwiched between indium, before firing.
Made from [indium][n-type Ge][indium] + copper. Fire it in a furnace to get an alloy-junction transistor.
At about 500 °C the indium melts and dissolves a little germanium. On cooling the Ge recrystallizes with indium inside it, forming a p-type layer. Doing it from both sides gives p-n-p.
How deep the two indium dots alloy in sets the base width. Controlling both sides at once was hard, so bases could not be made much thinner than 10 to a few tens of µm.
Germanium with a tiny bit of extra electrons.

Ge bonds to its neighbours with 4 electrons. A group-15 phosphorus atom (5 electrons) has one left over, which moves freely and carries current. Even one P atom per hundred million Ge atoms changes the conductivity greatly.
The n stands for negative: the carriers are negatively charged electrons. Early Bell Labs n-type Ge often used antimony or arsenic, but phosphorus is a genuine n-type dopant for Ge too.
Germanium a tiny bit short of electrons.
A group-13 indium atom (3 electrons) leaves one bond missing - a hole. When a neighbouring electron hops in, the hole appears to move, acting just like a moving positive charge.
The p stands for positive. The idea of the hole came from Peierls and Heisenberg around 1929-31, to explain metals whose Hall effect looked as if positive charges were flowing.
item.semiconductor-lab.refined_germanium: Extremely pure germanium, the stuff transistors are made of.

Zone refining: most impurities prefer the liquid to the solid (segregation coefficient k < 1). Sweep the molten zone the same way again and again, the impurities pile up at one end, and that end is cut off.
Invented by William Pfann at Bell Labs in 1952. A few passes brought impurities down to nearly one in ten billion (10N), giving the first material good enough for mass-produced transistors.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note1: The world's first transistor: a small current controls a big one.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note2: Made from 2 gold ingots + n-type germanium + copper.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note3: Two gold contacts, a few tens of µm apart, are pressed onto an n-type Ge slab by a plastic wedge. Holes injected at one (the emitter) strongly change the current at the other (the collector) - the signal was amplified up to about 100 times.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note4: Bardeen and Brattain at Bell Labs got it working on 16 December 1947, demonstrated it on the 23rd and announced it on 30 June 1948. The story goes that gold foil was wrapped round the wedge and slit at the tip with a razor to make the gap (⚠️ details unconfirmed). They shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with Shockley.
block.semiconductor-lab.zone_refining_fu: For silicon a graphite boat cannot be used (silicon reacts with it to form SiC), so the floating-zone method (around 1953) was developed: the bar stands upright and surface tension alone holds the molten zone.
block.semiconductor-lab.crystal_puller.n: Like cotton candy, it 'pulls' a crystal up out of molten germanium.

Uses 3 kW (built-in HF oscillator). Top left: refined germanium; middle: the seed; bottom left: hydrogen bags (also pulled from an adjacent gas holder). With tungsten wire as the seed, 1 Ge makes a seed crystal (30 s, the wire is used up); with a seed crystal, 4 Ge make a single-crystal ingot (60 s, the seed comes back). Purity and route carry over to the ingot.

A graphite crucible (germanium does not react with carbon) is kept just above Ge's melting point of about 938 °C by HF induction heating. In hydrogen, which prevents oxidation, a seed crystal is dipped into the melt and slowly pulled up while turning. The liquid freezes copying the seed's atomic arrangement, so the whole bar becomes one crystal. Real pull rates are 1-4 cm per hour, at 3-20 turns per minute.

The method itself was found in 1916 by the Pole Jan Czochralski while measuring how fast metal crystals grow (the story that he dipped his pen into molten tin instead of ink is unconfirmed). Teal and Little at Bell Labs used it for semiconductors in 1950. Told that polycrystals were good enough, Teal spent over a year persuading management - and single crystals made transistor performance uniform almost overnight.
gui.semiconductor-lab.crystal_puller.nee: Insert a seed (W wire or seed crystal)
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_seed_cr: A small piece of germanium with its atoms lined up perfectly - a 'model' for the crystal to copy.
Made in the crystal puller with tungsten wire in the seed slot (the very first one). Used as the seed when pulling single crystals, and not used up.

The first seed comes from grain selection: polycrystal forms on the tip of a thin wire, and pulling it out thin lets only the fastest-growing grain survive. After that, the end of a finished crystal is cut off to seed the next one. The seed's orientation sets the orientation of the whole ingot.

In 1959 W. C. Dash at GE found that necking the crystal down very thin just below the seed, then widening it again, lets defects (dislocations) grow out, giving dislocation-free crystals (Dash necking). Every silicon crystal today still starts from that thin neck.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_single_: A bar of germanium that is one single crystal throughout.
From the crystal puller: a seed crystal + 4 refined germanium. Purity and route stay as they were. More uses will come, e.g. the grown-junction transistor [9-10].

A polycrystal is a patchwork of small crystals pointing different ways. Electrons and holes are easily lost at the boundaries (grain boundaries), so properties vary from place to place. A single crystal has no grain boundaries: carriers live longer (long minority-carrier lifetime) and every slice behaves the same.

Teal moved to Texas Instruments in 1952 and in 1954 used crystal pulling to make silicon grown-junction transistors. The single-crystal technique that began with germanium became the doorway to the silicon age.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note1: Melts very pure silicon and slowly pulls one huge crystal out of it, like candy floss on a stick.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note2: 150 kW (graphite heater). Seed: polysilicon in the seed slot + quartz crucible + argon 1 → silicon seed crystal (60 s). Ingot: seed crystal (kept) + polysilicon 2 + quartz crucible + argon 2 (+ B2O3 for p-type or phosphorus for n-type, or nothing for intrinsic) → silicon single crystal (835 s = 17.4 kWh/kg). Crucibles are used once. Pulls argon from an adjacent gas holder. Real growers add the dopant as small chips of silicon containing a lot of B or P (master alloy).
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note3: Silicon melts at 1414 °C and reacts with graphite (forming SiC), so the crucible is quartz. The quartz slowly dissolves into the melt, so CZ crystals contain oxygen (about 10^18 atoms per cm³). Argon keeps air out and carries away the SiO that boils off. Boron enters the crystal almost evenly (segregation coefficient about 0.8); phosphorus mostly stays in the melt (about 0.35), so the bottom of an n-type ingot is more strongly doped.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note4: Jan Czochralski found the method in 1916 while measuring how fast metals crystallize. Today's ingots are 300 mm across and about 2 m long, weighing a few hundred kilograms. In 1959 Dash showed that pulling a very thin neck first removes the dislocations ⚠️. Most of the world's silicon wafers are made this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.placeh: ⚠️ Approximation: pulling is about 8× faster than real (about 1 mm per minute; the energy matches 17.4 kWh/kg). Argon amount is symbolic (real: tens of mol per kg). The dopant goes in directly as B2O3 / phosphorus; real growers add a master alloy (silicon chips with lots of B or P) ⚠️. Diameter control and oxygen amount are not modelled.

item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_crucible.n: A glass-like bowl of pure quartz that can hold molten silicon.
Fused quartz ×5 (U shape). Used once per pull in the CZ puller [9-08].
Silicon would react with a graphite crucible and turn into SiC, so silicon is melted in quartz (SiO2). The quartz softens near 1420 °C and slowly dissolves, adding oxygen to the crystal.
Real crucibles crack when the leftover silicon cools and expands, so each one is used for only one pull.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_crucible.p: Approximation: real crucibles are made by fusing high-purity quartz sand in a spinning mould with an electric arc; here it is crafted from fused quartz.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_seed_crys: A small piece of perfect crystal. The big crystal copies its direction.
Made in the CZ puller from a polysilicon tip. Used again and again (not used up) to grow single crystals.
When you dip the seed into the melt and pull, atoms line up following the seed. Pulling a thin neck first lets only one grain and no dislocations survive.
Real seeds are cut from earlier crystals in a chosen direction (such as <100>), and the direction decides the wafer's surface.
Approximation: the crystal direction is not shown.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_single_cr: One giant crystal of silicon. All its atoms line up in the same direction.
From the CZ puller [9-08]: polysilicon 2 → 1 ingot (about 2 kg). Purity comes from the polysilicon; B2O3 makes it p-type, phosphorus n-type. Next it is sliced into wafers [9-12].
In polycrystals, electrons scatter at grain boundaries; in a single crystal every transistor behaves the same. CZ crystals contain oxygen from the quartz crucible.

Boron spreads almost evenly from top to bottom (k ≈ 0.8), but phosphorus piles up toward the bottom (k ≈ 0.35), so an n-type ingot's resistance changes along its length. Oxygen is a weakness, but small oxygen clusters can also trap metal impurities (gettering).
Approximation: 1 ingot ≈ 2 kg; real ingots are a few hundred kg. Uneven doping along the ingot and oxygen are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note1: A spinning steel disc with diamonds on its edge slices a silicon crystal into thin plates.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note2: 1 kW (motor). Silicon single crystal 1 → silicon slices 8 (60 s). Purity and dopant pass to the slices. One diamond saw blade lasts 4 ingots.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note3: Silicon is hard and brittle, so it is ground away by diamond, the hardest material. The width of the blade turns into powder (kerf loss), so a good part of the ingot is lost.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note4: In 1954 Bell Labs cut long strips from a crystal to make the first practical solar cells. Later came inner-diameter saws (1970s) and multi-wire saws that cut hundreds of wafers at once (1990s), which need precision stages.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ Power (1 kW), time (60 s), 8 slices per ingot and blade life are game values (no source). Wafer thickness and the powder are not shown.
gui.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.need_inp: Needs a crystal and a blade
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw_blade: A steel disc with diamonds stuck around its edge.
Steel ingot + diamond ×4. Used in the wafer saw [9-12]; one blade lasts 4 ingots.
Only something harder than silicon can cut it cleanly. Diamond (pure carbon) is the hardest natural material; the diamonds slowly fall out as the blade wears.
Real blades use many tiny industrial diamonds bonded to the rim, not whole gems.
Approximation: real blades use diamond grit, not whole diamonds.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_wafer.not: A thin plate cut from a silicon crystal. Solar cells and chips are made on it.
From the wafer saw [9-12]: 8 per ingot, same purity and dopant as the ingot. Next: diffusion furnace [9-16] to make a p-n junction.
Because the whole slice is one crystal, every part behaves the same. The 1954 solar cells used long strips; today's wafers are round, 300 mm across and under 1 mm thick.
Modern wafers are lapped, etched and mirror-polished [9-13] before use. The 1954 cells did not need a mirror finish.

block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_furnac: Bakes silicon slices so that a little boron or phosphorus soaks into their surface.

5 kW. Silicon slices 8 (n-type or p-type) + 1 dopant source of the opposite type → p-n junction slices 8 (120 s). n-type slices take B2O3 (boron makes a thin p-type top, like the 1954 cell); p-type slices take phosphorus. Undoped or same-type slices make no junction, so it will not run. (The real 1954 base was arsenic-doped n-type; the game uses phosphorus, also group V.)

At high temperature, dopant atoms wander slowly from the surface into the solid (diffusion, Fick's law). A thin layer of the other type forms on top, and where it meets the base is the p-n junction, the heart of solar cells and transistors.

In 1954 Fuller diffused boron into arsenic-doped (n-type) silicon to make the first practical solar cell. Earlier cells made with lithium were unstable because the lithium kept moving at room temperature. From 1955, an oxide mask let dopant enter only through chosen windows.

Omitted: ⚠️ Temperature (about 1000 °C), power (5 kW) and time (120 s; real diffusion takes hours) are game values not yet checked against sources. The real 1954 base was arsenic-doped; here phosphorus (also group V) is used because arsenic is not in the game yet. The carrier gas is omitted.
n + B → p-n / p + P → n-p
item.semiconductor-lab.pn_junction_wafer: A silicon slice with a thin layer of the other type on top. Light on it makes electricity.
From the diffusion furnace [9-16]. 8 of them + copper cable make a solar cell [B-12].
At the junction, electrons and holes are pulled apart by a built-in electric field. When light frees an electron, the field pushes it one way and the hole the other: that is a current.
The same p-n junction is inside every diode and transistor. A solar cell is a big, flat diode that faces the sun.
Approximation: junction depth and the thin top layer are not modelled.
A battery radio that fits in your pocket.

Alloy-junction transistor ×3 (amplify) + graphite (carbon resistor) + copper cable (tuning/antenna coil) + Leyden jar (capacitor) + magnet (speaker) + zinc ingot and graphite rod (zinc-carbon battery: zinc can and carbon rod). The goal of chapter 1. No redstone: every part is a real radio part.

It picks one station out of the weak signals from the antenna (tuning), extracts the audio (detection) and amplifies it with transistors to drive the speaker. Unlike tubes there is no warm-up, so it plays at once and the battery lasts.

The Regency TR-1 (USA, 1954, four transistors) was the first commercial transistor radio. Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (later Sony) released the TR-55 in 1955, and its 1957 TR-63 sold worldwide as a 'pocketable' radio.

⚠️ Approximation: the capacitor is a Leyden jar (real radios use small paper, ceramic or electrolytic capacitors). The battery is only its zinc can and carbon rod (the real zinc-carbon cell also needs MnO2 and an ammonium chloride paste, not in the game yet). The speaker cone, ferrite antenna rod and plastic case are omitted. The TR-1 had 4 transistors; here 3.
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note1: A silicon panel that turns sunlight straight into electricity. The goal of chapter 2!
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note2: p-n junction slices 8 + copper cable. Gives 60 W in daytime under open sky (glass is fine), about 12 W (20%) on rainy, cloudy days from scattered light, and 0 at night or under a roof. Right-click to see the output. Connect with copper cable like other generators. The real 1954 cell had an arsenic-doped n-type base (the game uses phosphorus).
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note3: Noon sunlight is about 1000 W per m². With 6% efficiency, a 1 m² block gives 60 W. In 1954 Bell Labs said its cells could deliver about 50 W per square yard, which matches.
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.note4: On 25 April 1954 Chapin, Fuller and Pearson showed the 'Bell Solar Battery' running a toy Ferris wheel. The 1954 cell used a dull plastic film to stop reflection, and both contacts were on the back. In 1958 cells powered the satellite Vanguard 1. Today's home panels reach over 20%.
block.semiconductor-lab.solar_cell.place: Approximation: output does not change with the sun's height or cloud thickness (only day/night and rain; rain = 20% ⚠️, real overcast light varies). The n-type base is phosphorus, not arsenic as in 1954 ⚠️. Electrodes are copper cable (the 1954 electrode metal is not yet checked ⚠️). Reflection coating omitted.

item.minecraft.charcoal.note1: Black, light charcoal, made by burning wood with little air.
item.minecraft.charcoal.note2: Smelt logs in a furnace (vanilla). In this MOD it is the carbon for reducing germanium dioxide (GeO2 + C) and for making phosphorus, and fuel for fires and furnaces.
item.minecraft.charcoal.note3: Heating wood to about 400-700 °C with the air shut off (dry distillation) drives out water and the volatile matter that would become smoke, leaving charcoal of 80-90% carbon. Unlike coal it contains almost no sulfur, so it reduces metals without contaminating them.
item.minecraft.charcoal.note4: The black lines of cave paintings were drawn with charcoal over 30,000 years ago. In England, where too much forest had been cut to make iron, Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke (baked coal) in 1709, ending the charcoal age. Japan's binchotan is a hard white charcoal born in Edo-period Kishu.
